title: adapter-boundary-routing-notes
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working sketch to clarify service boundaries and ownership for the control plane router surface in multi-region deployments. Focus areas: API gateway responsibilities, orchestration/policy engine role, and runtime adapter contracts (what adapters must expose so the control plane can make routing decisions). The goal is to produce a minimal operational spec teams can adopt without stifling implementation choices.

Context and motivation:
- We have recurring incidents where routing decisions blur ownership between gateway, control-plane orchestration, and runtime adapters (examples in PLAT-873).
- Multi-region deployments add complexity: region affinity, cached KV state, and legal/data residency constraints must be enforced by routing.
- Need a clear handoff model so SRE, platform, and serving-runtime teams have crisp responsibilities. This doc sketches a territory model and a set of invariants.

High-level territory model (conceptual):
- Ingress Tier (API Gateway): auth, coarse request classification, tenant/route lookup, initial policy enforcement. Fast path only.
- Control Plane (Orchestration / Policy Engine): decision-making layer — chooses target adapter(s), applies capacity-aware routing, failover logic, rollout policies, and selects model variant.
- Runtime Adapters (Adapter Layer): expose capability manifests and live capacity signals; accept forwarded requests and report outcomes, traces, and telemetry.
- Observability & Ops: cross-cutting — consumes events from all three layers and owns UI/alerts.

Responsibilities (short bullets):
- API Gateway owns:
  - Authentication + authorization, rate limiting, and request enrichment (tenant id, route id).
  - Fast classification: tag requests by workload profile (short-chat, long-context, embeddings, rerank).
  - Enforce safety and policy-level blocking (deny lists) that must be applied before routing.
  - Provide a stable, documented interface to the control plane (route lookup RPC, request preview).
- Control Plane orchestration owns:
  - Routing policy evaluation (latency-first, cost-first, capacity-aware, region-affinity).
  - Rollouts and canary policies (per-model and per-tenant).
  - Fallback strategies (model variant, region, degraded feature sets).
  - Persisting routing decisions for audit and replay; understanding cache invalidation semantics.
  - Owning the ‘route catalogue’ and rule precedence.
- Runtime Adapters own:
  - Capability manifest (supported model families, quantization profiles, max sequence lengths, hardware hints).
  - Live capacity and health signals (load, queue length, estimated per-token latency).
  - Correct execution of dispatched requests and deterministic error semantics.
  - Providing KV/prefix cache compatibility marker when appropriate.

Adapter capability manifest (proposal):
- adapter_id: string (unique)
- supported_workloads: comma-separated list (generation, chat, embeddings, batching-allowed)
- peak_tokens_per_sec: numeric string
- region: primary region code
- supports_kv_cache: yes|no
- quantization_profiles: comma-separated labels

Note: above fields would be expressed as a simple schema the runtime adapter registers on boot. Control plane uses them in decision trees.

Routing policy primitives (to be consumed by orchestration):
- affinity(region|data_residency|hardware_tier)
- preference(latency|cost|throughput)
- capability_required(list)
- fallback_sequence(list of adapter_ids or adapters by capability)

Decision flow (per-request):
1) Gateway authenticates and tags request. If blocked by policy -> 403.
2) Gateway calls control-plane route-eval RPC with request metadata and optional tenant hints.
3) Control plane queries latest adapter manifests + capacity cache. Evaluate policies: affinity, hard constraints (data residency), then soft preferences.
4) Select primary adapter and a prioritized fallback list (for fast failover). Persist decision to audit log.
5) Return chosen adapter endpoint(s) to gateway. Gateway forwards request (or proxies stream) to adapter(s).
6) Adapter responds; telemetry + outcome events flow back to observability.

Multi-region and data residency considerations:
- Hard constraints (legal) must be enforced in control plane: if tenant has EU-only requirement, adapters outside EU are ineligible for selection.
- Region affinity time-window: default 15m sticky to the last adapter selected for the tenant+route unless overridden by capacity. This reduces cache miss and KV cache churn.
- Cross-region fallback: prefer cold failover (route to other region) only if latency SLO allows or request is non-sensitive.
- When shifting an active workload between regions, orchestrator guarantees a versioned rollout and ensures KV prefix compatibility (migration checklist).

Ownership table (working sketch):
- API Gateway: Platform-API team — SLO: 99.95% ingress path. Owns auth, initial policy enforcement, WAF rules.
- Control Plane / Orchestrator: Platform-Engine team — SLO: 99.9% decision latency < 50ms for cached manifests. Owns route catalogue, rollout automation.
- Adapter Interface & Runtime: Serving-Runtime team — SLO: 99.9% request execution availability per adapter. Owns adapter manifests and telemetry contract.
- Observability & Tracing: Observability team — SLO: 99% event delivery within 60s. Owns UX for tracing routed decisions.

Soft vs hard boundaries:
- Hard boundary example: Data residency — control plane must never choose an adapter outside allowed regions (hard constraint).
- Soft boundary example: Cost preferences — policy may prefer cheaper adapters but will choose higher-cost option when latency SLO is threatened.

Telemetry and audit requirements:
- Every routing decision must emit an event: {request_id, tenant_id, route_id, selected_adapter, fallback_list, timestamp, policy_version}.
- Adapters must emit enriched completion events: {request_id, outcome_code, lat_ms, tokens_in/out, adapter_manifest_version}.
- Orchestrator must retain route decision traces for 30 days (default) with easy mapping to incidents.

Operational playbooks (short):
- Adapter outage: control plane should mark adapter unhealthy and promote next fallback; notify serving-runtime on-call; rollback any canary traffic to previous variant. (JIRA: ENG-4021 sample incident)
- Region blackout: run regional-failover checklist: ban new rollouts in impacted region, fail traffic to warm pool, enforce data residency tagging.
- Unclear routing behavior: toggle route-eval verbose logging and capture sample traces; create PLAT ticket with sample request ids.

Open questions / unresolved decisions:
- Will the gateway proxy streaming (saves client <-> adapter connection) or only handoff adapter endpoint? Tradeoffs: connection churn vs routing transparency.
- Should the orchestrator do predictive pre-warming based on historical TTLs (for bursty tenants)? Who pays for pre-warm cost?
- Where do we accept and persist per-tenant overrides for routing (customer-facing controls)? DB or config?

Next steps / action items:
- (Asha) Draft minimal adapter manifest schema; share with serving-runtime for feedback by 2024-10-02.
- (Diego) Prototype route-eval RPC payload and latency budget measurement PR (github PR 1284) — due 2024-10-16.
- (Lin) Run a tabletop for region-failover playbook with SRE and security — schedule week of 2024-10-09.

Appendix: quick sample route-eval payload (informal)
{
  "tenant_id": "tid-123",
  "route_id": "text-gen-v2",
  "workload": "generation",
  "affinity": "eu-preferred",
  "hard_constraints": ["eu_only"],
  "preference": "latency",
  "max_latency_ms": 120
}

Notes-to-self:
- Keep this doc intentionally lightweight. We will evolve into a confluence page CP-Routing-API once teams validate schema.
- Capture any regulatory constraints as policy modules the control plane evaluates (avoid ad-hoc checks in gateway).

References and tickets:
- PLAT-873: routing ownership confusion — incident postmortem link in Confluence
- ENG-4021: adapter crash scenario and suggested fallback behavior
- GitHub PR: platform/pull/1284 (route-eval message sketch)
